**Python cache. Rust engine. SQLite storage.**

Every Python web app arrives at the same crossroads. A query that was fine at launch is now the slowest thing on the page, so you cache its result in a dict, and for one afternoon you're a hero. Then the app goes under gunicorn with four workers, and there are four dicts, each warming up alone and each forgetting everything the moment its worker is recycled. So you reach for Redis, and now there's a server to deploy, secure, monitor and pay for, whose entire job is to remember the answer to one query.

[python-diskcache](https://github.com/grantjenks/python-diskcache) showed there was a third road: a cache that is just a directory. Every thread and every process on the machine opens the same path and sees the same entries, and the entries are still there tomorrow, because a directory doesn't restart. No daemon, no network hop, no second system to keep alive. It's the kind of idea that sounds too simple to be fast, and for years that was the catch. diskcache itself has had no commits since 2023, and its issues and pull requests go unanswered.

diskcache-oxide removes the catch. It keeps the diskcache API you already know and rebuilds everything beneath it for where Python is going: many cores, many worker processes, free-threaded CPython, and async frameworks that can't afford a slow call on the event loop. The engine is Rust. The storage is SQLite. The Python layer is as thin as it can be. One thread gets nearly 600,000 cache operations a second out of a `Cache`, and eight threads sharing it still get that rate while python-diskcache's falls below 20,000. Nothing on your disk is a pickle unless you asked for one, and memory and disk use stay where you set them.

**Source on GitHub: <https://github.com/mikeckennedy/diskcache-oxide>** · [Issues](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/diskcache-oxide/issues)

Here is the whole idea on one screen. Four workers, one directory. The cache makes the slow query cheap, and `add()` elects exactly one worker to run the hourly job, because a write that's atomic across processes is a lock if you squint:

```python
import os

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

# Every worker process opens the same directory and sees the same cache.
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')

def popular_episodes() -> list[dict]:
    if (episodes := cache.get('episodes:popular')) is not None:
        return episodes
    episodes = db.load_popular_episodes()
    cache.set('episodes:popular', episodes, expire=300)
    return episodes

# Only one worker in the whole fleet runs the hourly job: add() is atomic across processes.
if cache.add('job:refresh-feeds', os.getpid(), expire=3600):
    refresh_feeds()

cache.close()  # at shutdown
```

And here is what it does under load. Every thread shares one cache, the x axis adds threads, and the two libraries go in opposite directions:

::: {.dco-chart data-type="lines" data-x-labels="1,2,4,8" data-x="threads" data-y="operations per second" data-unit="ops/s" data-title="Eight threads on one cache: diskcache's throughput collapses, diskcache-oxide's holds" data-note="bench/gate.py on an 18-core Apple M5 Pro, Python 3.14 with the GIL, four interleaved rounds, the 0.2.3 code (bench/results/macos/gate-3.14.txt). Higher is better; hover for the numbers."}
| Mix | diskcache-oxide | diskcache 5.6.3 |
|---|---|---|
| 99 reads to 1 write | 589k / 578k / 580k / 568k | 375k / 177k / 58k / 15k |
| 1,000 reads to 1 write | 655k / 645k / 655k / 655k | 410k / 163k / 55k / 15k |
:::

## An app with several caches

Most apps end up with more than one cache: rendered pages, API responses, sessions, rate limits, each with its own size and settings. `Caches` is the registry for them. You register each cache once at startup, and a lookup by name opens it on first use and returns the same object every time after that. If a cache can't open (a full disk, a permissions problem, a cache left behind by an older release), the lookup returns a `NullCache` instead of raising, so requests carry on without that cache while the error is logged, and the registry tries again every 10 seconds until the real one is back. One call switches a cache off for a load test, and `stats()` gives an admin page every cache's entries, size and errors.

```python
from diskcache_oxide import Caches

caches = Caches('/var/cache/my-app', timeout=1.0)  # settings here apply to every cache
caches.register('pages', size_limit=2 * 2**30)
caches.register('sessions', eviction_policy='none')  # never evicted for size
caches.register('rate_limits', shards=8)  # a FanoutCache, for many writers

html = caches['pages'].get('/about')  # opens on first use, the same object after that
caches['sessions'].set('session:9f2c', {'user': 42}, expire=3600)
caches.fanout('rate_limits').incr('ip:203.0.113.7')

caches.disable('pages')  # a load test without the page cache: no call site changes

for name, stat in caches.stats().items():  # for an admin page
    print(name, stat.count, stat.volume, stat.error)

caches.close_all()  # at shutdown
```

Talk Python runs its eight caches this way. [Named caches](user-guide/caches.qmd) covers the registry in full.

## Where this is going

diskcache-oxide is being built in three stages. The first is done and the second is mostly done.

1. **A better diskcache.** The `Cache` and [`FanoutCache`](user-guide/fanoutcache.qmd) you already know, rebuilt in Rust: about half the read latency, many times the threaded throughput, safe across `fork()`, safe on free-threaded Python, and no pickle by default.
2. **The complete local caching toolkit.** Keys of every native type, `memoize`, [tags](recipes/invalidating-groups.qmd), [work queues](recipes/work-queues.qmd), [`transact()`](user-guide/transactions.qmd) and the [coordination recipes](user-guide/coordination.qmd) (locks, semaphores, throttles, stampede protection) are all here. Still to come in this stage are a Django cache backend, free-threaded scaling, and a native `AsyncCache` for FastAPI, Litestar and friends.
3. **A cache server.** The same Rust engine served over the network: a Redis-style central cache for a fleet of machines, with SQLite underneath instead of RAM. As the only owner of its files, the server can use SQLite's exclusive locking mode, which already measures about 40% faster reads than the shared-directory library.

See [Vision and roadmap](user-guide/roadmap.qmd) for how each stage breaks down.

## Why diskcache-oxide

- **[Fast where web apps spend their time.](user-guide/performance.qmd)** At a 99:1 read/write mix, one thread gets about 590,000 operations a second from a `Cache`, 1.6× diskcache's rate and cheap enough to call straight from the event loop. Add threads and the gap opens: at 8 threads on a GIL build, diskcache's per-thread connections pile into each other and its throughput falls to 15,000 a second, while oxide's stays near 570,000, 38× ahead (the chart above).
- **[Built for free-threaded Python.](user-guide/concurrency-and-forks.qmd)** The extension is compiled with `gil_used = false` and never leans on the GIL for correctness, which matters on a build where there's no GIL to lean on. Every change is tested on 3.14, 3.14t, 3.15 and 3.15t.
- **[Safe across `fork()`.](user-guide/concurrency-and-forks.qmd)** gunicorn, Celery's prefork pool and `multiprocessing` create workers by copying the parent, and the copy includes whatever SQLite lock a thread was holding at that instant. A process-wide fork barrier makes sure no child is ever born holding half a transaction.
- **[No pickle on your disk.](user-guide/serialization.qmd)** Values are msgpack (or JSON) with exact type tags, so tuples, sets, datetimes, dates, Decimals, big ints and NaN come back as what you stored, not as whatever the format could manage. Your own types are registered once and read back only where the name is registered. Pickle is opt-in, and a cache that didn't opt in refuses to unpickle anything it finds, however it got there.
- **[Predictable memory and disk.](user-guide/storage-and-wal.qmd)** A bounded connection pool, a 1 MiB page cache per connection, a write-ahead log that trims itself back down, and a `checkpoint()` for when you want it empty now.
- **[Correct under pressure.](user-guide/divergences.qmd)** `clear()` never deletes writes that landed while it ran, a reader racing an overwrite gets the old value or the new one, never a spurious miss, and a queue never hands a worker another queue's items or loses one it couldn't read. Running the same test suite against both libraries turned up 18 bugs in diskcache, each with a reproduction in the repo, and each fixed here.
- **[More than get and set.](user-guide/coordination.qmd)** `memoize` caches a function's results by its arguments. Tags group entries so `evict(tag)` removes a user's or a page's in one call. `push` and `pull` make a [work queue](recipes/work-queues.qmd) every worker shares, handing each item to exactly one of them. Locks, semaphores and rate limits hold across every process on the machine, with no Redis.
- **[A real off switch.](user-guide/null-cache.qmd)** `NullCache` turns caching off without a single `if cache is not None:` in your code, and can keep forwarding invalidations to the real cache while it's off, so nothing stale is waiting when you turn it back on.
- **[Named caches with an off switch.](user-guide/caches.qmd)** `Caches` registers an app's caches once, opens each on first use, hands out a `NullCache` while one can't open, and gives an admin page its counts and sizes.
- **[Errors you can act on.](user-guide/errors.qmd)** Every exception says what went wrong, in words, and the errors page says what to do about it. Nothing is swallowed unless you turned on the setting that swallows it.
- **Typed.** Ships `py.typed` and a `CacheLike` protocol that `Cache`, `FanoutCache` and `NullCache` all satisfy.

## Status

::: {.callout-note}
diskcache-oxide runs in production at [Talk Python](https://talkpython.fm), [Python Bytes](https://pythonbytes.fm) and [Talk Python Training](https://training.talkpython.fm). Every release runs three gauntlets first. A conformance suite runs the same tests against diskcache 5.6.3 itself, and every place the two differ is a deliberate decision, written down with its reason in [Divergences](user-guide/divergences.qmd). A sanitizer pass puts the whole codebase, bundled SQLite included, under Miri, ThreadSanitizer (with a free-threaded CPython built under it too), AddressSanitizer and LeakSanitizer. And a 24-hour soak throws processes, threads, forks, `SIGKILL` and `clear()` under load at one directory for a day, then checks it for corruption, lost writes and leaks.

Most of diskcache's API is here: `Cache` and `FanoutCache`, keys of every native type, `memoize`, tags and `evict()`, `transact()`, the queue calls `push`, `pull` and `peek`, `retry=`, `stats()`, `check()`, `eviction_policy='none'`, and the coordination recipes. Still to come: `Deque` and `Index`, reading a large value as a file (`read=`), `AsyncCache`, a Django cache backend, and Windows. Custom `disk=` classes and least-recently-used eviction aren't coming; [Vision and roadmap](user-guide/roadmap.qmd) says why.
:::

## Install

```bash
pip install diskcache-oxide
```

It supports CPython 3.14 and 3.15, including the free-threaded builds (3.14t and 3.15t), on macOS and Linux. Wheels cover macOS on Apple Silicon and Linux (glibc) on x86_64 and aarch64 for all four Pythons, with the compiled engine and a bundled SQLite inside, so there's nothing else to install. Anywhere else pip builds from source, which needs the latest stable Rust toolchain. Windows support is planned.

Before 1.0, a release that changes the on-disk format bumps the minor version and says so first in its changelog entry: delete your caches when you upgrade to it. Until you do, opening one raises `FormatMismatchError`, which names the file. It's a cache, so the cost is a cold start.

## Coming from diskcache?

Change the import and point it at a new directory. That's the migration. diskcache-oxide keeps diskcache's API but uses its own file format (`diskcache-oxide.sqlite`), so it never reads or touches an existing `cache.db`:

```python
# from diskcache import Cache
from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-oxide')
```

[Switching from diskcache](user-guide/switching-from-diskcache.qmd) covers every difference you might notice, which is mostly things getting better and now and then things getting stricter.
